       Jerome and Gaylynn Sneed timely submit1 the following Exceptions to the Proposal for

Decision (“PFD”) issued by the State Office of Administrative Hearings (“SOAH”) Administrative

Law Judges (“ALJs”) on August 20, 2026, and would respectfully show as follows:


                            I.      INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY

       The Sneeds thank the ALJs for their careful and thoughtful consideration of the need for

this CCN. The PFD correctly recommends that the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“PUCT”

or “Commission”) deny the Application. Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA

Transmission Services Corporation (collectively, “Applicants”) failed to establish that the Project

 is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public under Public

Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) § 37.056, as well as failed to comply with due process. 2

except to the PFD’s recommendation to use Route 894.3 As a result of the lack of due process,

Staff and the ALJs were deprived of the ability to review the entire record testimony and evidence.

Had more time been provided, they would have likely found that the unrebutted record evidence

identifies Route 891 as the superior route on nearly every routing criterion the Commission must

consider. However, the PFD’s routing analysis only addressed the Route in a single paragraph

that concludes, without further analysis, that Route 891 does not “present a clear advantage over

the Focus Routes4 overall such that it should be given serious consideration.”5 Route 891 in fact

does present clear advantages over Routes 894 and 487 on the most essential Commission routing

criteria:

        Route 891 is the most fair to landowners and most reasonable to ratepayers. When the

PUCT’s routing criteria point clearly toward an alternative route, the Commission should follow

them. The Sneeds respectfully except to the PFD’s routing recommendation as set forth below

and request that, should the Commission approve the Application, it select Route 891 rather than

Route 894 or any other route utilizing Link G13.


II.      THE PFD CORRECTLY FINDS THAT APPLICANTS FAILED TO ESTABLISH
                   NEED AND FAILED TO PROVIDE DUE PROCESS

        The PFD concludes that Applicants failed to establish that the Bell County East-to-Big Hill

Project is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public within

 the meaning of PURA § 37.056,8 and separately concludes that Applicants failed to provide due

process in multiple respects.9 The Sneeds agree with and support both conclusions.

        1. Applicants Failed to Establish Need

        When approving the Permian Basin Reliability Plan, the Commission made clear in its

order that applicants “must establish in the CCN proceeding that the certificate meets all applicable

legal requirements for a CCN, including the requirement set forth in PURA § 37.056(a) that the

certificate is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.” 10

Instead of independently establishing need in each CCN proceeding as the Commission ordered,

Applicants seem to merely point to the existence of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan. This

circular justification is plainly inadequate.

        Furthermore, the Permian Basin Reliability Plan fails to establish need for the project.

ERCOT has acknowledged miscalculations in the load forecast underpinning the Plan, 11 Staff has

stated “changes are needed” to the forecast, 12 and the PUCT has found that the forecast is

unrealistic.13 In addition to inaccurate load assumptions, there has been no showing that generation

capacity is available in central or eastern Texas to export to the Permian Basin 14—the stated

         2. Intervenors Were Fundamentally Deprived of Due Process

         The PFD correctly concludes that the “burdens and deprivations [imposed on intervenors]

are not independent but cumulative,” and that the failure of due process in this proceeding “is not

about one measure in isolation—it is about their convergence.” 16 In addition to those due process

failures highlighted in the PFD,17 affected landowners were deprived of both the information

needed to meaningfully participate and the time to be heard.

         First, Applicants failed to give the Sneeds notice of the basic physical characteristics of the

facilities they propose to construct across the Sneed Ranch—even when requested through

discovery.18       Landowners cannot meaningfully evaluate, prepare for, or contest a 765-kV

transmission line through the center of their property when the Applicants refuse to disclose how

many towers will be built, how tall they will be, where they will stand, whether and how they will

be lit, the noise levels landowners will endure at their home, the herbicides that will be applied to

landowners’ property, or the health impacts imposed by the project. 19 These concerns were raised

in both Mr. Sneed’s Direct Testimony20 and in the Sneeds’ First Set of Requests for Information

This is a proceeding in which the Sneeds “may be deprived of property rights and hence notice

eminent domain.             The constitutional minimum in such a proceeding is “notice reasonably

and afford them an opportunity to present their objections.” 25 Notice that satisfies due process

must be “more than a mere gesture”; the means employed of informing a party “must be such as

the leading route, Route 891, as the route best balancing key factors of paralleling property

boundaries, minimizing cost, avoiding sensitive watersheds, and mitigating impacts to habitable

structures. This is understandable given the volume of evidence on the record—Staff itself, who

spent weeks reviewing testimony, had not yet been able to reach the testimony of Mr. Sneed or the

expert testimony of Ms. Hubbard, which clearly identify Route 891 as the superior alternative,

before filing Staff’s recommendation33 and taking the stand at the final hearing. 34 Even so,

Commission Staff’s witness confirmed on cross-examination that, while he did not analyze Route

891 before forming his recommendation, once presented with the data it was clear that Route 891

outperforms Route 296—a route Staff otherwise regarded as superior to Route 894—on multiple

key criteria, including paralleling property boundaries and cost. 35

         Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B) directs the Commission to weigh paralleling, cost, environmental

integrity, moderation of impact on landowners, and other enumerated factors in selecting “the best

alternative” route.48 A recommendation that omits analysis of Route 891, which is supported by

conclude that Route 894 is, in fact, superior to Route 891. The Sneeds except to the PFD’s routing

        2. Route 891 Bisects Fewer Miles of Landowner Property Than Routes 894, 487 and
           All Other Routes of Interest

        The most meaningful measure of landowner impact is the degree to which a route follows

the boundaries of a property, rather than bisecting or trisecting the interior. As Chairman Gleeson

said in a recent proceeding, “the integrity of [ranches and farms] should be preserved and property

boundaries respected whenever possible.”49           Because the Commission treats paralleling of

property lines as a substantive routing obligation rather than an aspirational goal, Route 891’s

leading performance on this criterion is a principal reason it is the strongest of the routes

recommended in this proceeding.

        Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B) explicitly requires the Commission to consider the extent to which a

route parallels property boundaries, 50 and it has long been the Commission’s policy to avoid

component from the compatible ROW component, it understates the degree to which Routes 894

and 487 impose unnecessary burdens on landowners.

39% for Route 487.58 In other words, Route 891 bisects fewer miles of landowner property than
